title: The Truth About Jowls (And What Actually Works)
excerpt: Jowls — that collection of loose skin and fat below the jawline — are one of the most frustrating aging concerns. And here's why: most of the products and treatments marketed to "fix" them don't actually work. Unlike fine lines or dark spots, jowls aren't just a skin-deep problem. They're structural.

title: Do All Skin Tones Need Sunscreen?
excerpt: Sunscreen has become a cornerstone of skincare advice, but if you have melanin-rich skin, you've probably wondered: do I really need it? The short answer is yes—UV protection isn't just for fair skin types.

title: What Does Broad Spectrum SPF Mean?
excerpt: If you've ever picked up a bottle of sunscreen, chances are you've seen the words "broad spectrum SPF" stamped on the label. But what does it mean? Let's break it down in a way that makes sense.

title: Is Azelaic Acid Worth the Hype?
excerpt: Azelaic acid is a naturally occurring dicarboxylic acid derived from grains such as barley, rye, and wheat. It also exists as a byproduct of Malassezia yeast, part of the skin’s microbiome and the cause of tinea versicolor. Azelaic acid is FDA-approved for the treatment of both acne and rosacea and has gained increasing popularity for use in hyperpigmentation and post-inflammatory erythema (PIE). There are now modified versions of azelaic acid on the market, such as Potassium Azeloyl Diglycinate (glycinated azelaic acid). They dissolve in water and have less published data on their own, so they work best alongside azelaic acid. When published evidence is limited, look for brands that have tested their finished formula in a third-party clinical study. Remedy's 15% Azelaic Acid Complex Advanced Clarifying Serum (10% pure azelaic acid + 5% glycinated azelaic acid) was clinically proven to improve dark spots and redness in 97.5% of participants in a single-center, dermatologist-evaluated clinical study (n=40).

title: Azelaic Acid for Post-Inflammatory Erythema (PIE)
excerpt: The breakout is gone. The red mark it left behind is not. Months later, you are still looking at a flat pink or red patch where a pimple used to be, and none of your dark spot products are touching it.

title: What Are Milia And What Actually Gets Rid of Them?
excerpt: Those small, hard white bumps under your eyes are not pimples. They will not respond to squeezing. And no, your pore strips won't touch them. They are milia — and they play by different rules.

title: Acanthosis Nigricans 101
excerpt: If you've noticed areas of your skin becoming darker, thicker, and velvety, particularly around the neck, underarms, or groin, you may be dealing with a common skin condition called acanthosis nigricans (AN). Though not harmful, it can be a visible sign of underlying health concerns that should not be ignored.

title: Understanding Cherry Angiomas
excerpt: Cherry angiomas are among the most common benign skin growths that people notice as they age, often small, bright red, and harmless, but sometimes bothersome for cosmetic reasons.

title: How to Use Azelaic Acid in Your Routine
excerpt: Azelaic acid is one of the easier actives to fit into a routine, largely because of what it does not do. It does not increase sun sensitivity. It does not require a buffering period the way retinoids often do. It does not conflict with most of what people are already using.

title: Skin Changes During Perimenopause
excerpt: Many women don't connect the dots right away. The breakouts, the dryness, the skin that suddenly feels different despite no change in routine. Perimenopause can start in your late 30s, and the skin feels it before most people expect it to.

title: Dark Circles: What Causes Them and What Actually Works
excerpt: Dark circles have multiple causes, and treating them effectively means identifying which one, or which combination, applies to you.

title: Microneedling 101
excerpt: Microneedling uses fine needles to create thousands of controlled micro-injuries in the skin. It sounds counterintuitive, but the controlled damage is the point. Here is how it works, what it treats, and how to approach it safely.

title: Solubilized Azelaic Acid vs Suspensions
excerpt: If you have used azelaic acid and found it gritty, chalky or oddly thick, that is not the ingredient. It is the formulation.

title: Glycinated Azelaic Acid, Explained
excerpt: On an ingredient list it appears as potassium azeloyl diglycinate. In marketing copy it is usually called glycinated azelaic acid. It is one of those ingredients people either skip past entirely or assume is a watered-down substitute for the real thing.

title: Azelaic Acid and Niacinamide
excerpt: Azelaic acid and niacinamide turn up together constantly, in the same routines and increasingly in the same bottle. They are compatible, they are both well tolerated, and they address overlapping concerns from different angles.

title: Can You Use Azelaic Acid With Tretinoin or Retinol?
excerpt: Short answer: yes. Azelaic acid and retinoids are one of the more compatible pairings in skincare, and dermatologists combine them routinely.
